title: Food photo hero in a loud brand voice
works: Full-width photo of the food in use
Large serif headline with one lime button
Bold yellow and cream sections keep the brand
fixes: Dark overlay makes the photo look dull
Phone view crops the product out
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens with a full-width photo of food being made and a plain headline that says what the product does. The brand colours and drawings appear in the sections below, so the page keeps its own voice.

## What works
- The hero photo shows real food and hands, so the visitor sees the product in use.
- The headline is short, in a large serif, and a single lime button sits under it.
- Yellow, cream and dark green blocks with drawn olive artwork make the page easy to remember.

## Where it is weak
- A dark layer over the hero photo makes the food look flat.
- On the phone the photo is cropped to a hand and bread, so the product is not shown.

## The lesson
Open with a photo of the product in use and a headline that says its benefit, then carry the brand colours through each section.

fixes: 'Here's how we do it' pill blends into the image
Body copy is small and low contrast on dark panels

- Each section has its own scene and color: sunset, a dark brown card, dusk purple, then a light blue band. Each section gets one short headline and a short paragraph, so the page moves along without feeling crowded.

## Where it is weak
- The 'Here's how we do it' pill is translucent and sits on a busy part of the house image, so it is hard to read. The same problem shows on the phone.
- The body text on the dark brown and purple panels is small and thin, and the orange-red text on brown is l

title: Laughing full-bleed photo with a handwritten word
works: Full-bleed laughing photo feels human
Yellow handwritten "recovery" adds warmth
Dropdown in the hero starts the visit
fixes: Hero dropdown text is small and faint
Round accessibility buttons sit over the photo
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero is a tight, joyful photo of two people laughing. The headline says "With the right care, recovery is a reality", with one word in yellow handwriting. A visitor feels hope before reading any detail.

## What works
- The photo fills the whole hero with a warm tint, and the white headline stays readable over it.
- A small handwritten arrow reading "start here" points to a white box that asks "Who do you want to help?". It sorts visitors at the first step.
- Below the hero come press logos, alumni videos on a purple band and numbers such as 85% rated their experience good to excellent.

## Where it is weak
- The text in the dropdown and the line under the headline is small and light for a key step.
- Two round buttons sit on the photo corner and compete with the content.

## The lesson
Put a single question box inside a full-bleed human photo so the visitor picks a path in the first screen.

title: Full-screen aircraft in flight, wide techno type
works: Real aircraft in flight fill the hero
Wide spaced type looks technical
Large product cards with clear Explore links
fixes: No clear button for a visitor to press
Phone crop cuts off the aircraft
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens with a full-width image of an electric aircraft flying under a moody sky. The headline "Building the future of aerospace and defense" is set in a wide, spaced typeface. The page reads as serious engineering, not a brochure.

## What works
- The hero shows the real product in the air. The brand has no need for stock images.
- The wide capital type is the same across the headline and product names, so the page has one clear voice.
- Large cards for Archer Halo and Midnight each hold one photo, one name, a short line and an "Explore" link.

## Where it is weak
- The hero has no button. A visitor must use the small menu to find a next step.
- On a phone the aircraft is cropped at the edge and the headline wraps into four short lines.

## The lesson
Let one large real photo of the product carry the page, then give it a button so the visitor has somewhere to go.

title: Illustrated world behind tilted question cards
works: Hand-drawn scene gives the brand a style
Tilted cards name real life questions
Red, cream and yellow palette stays tight
fixes: Tilted card text is harder to read
Phone page loses the illustrated scene early
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens on a cream background with a red serif headline: "Intuitive guidance for modern life". Tilted cards around it carry short lines such as "Someone to talk to 24/7". Below, a large hand-drawn landscape holds cards with everyday questions. The page feels friendly, not mystical.

## What works
- A stats pill shows 45M readings, 2,000+ vetted advisors and a 4.8/5 rating, with advisor faces and one dark button "Match with an advisor".
- The cards name real moments: moving away, being left on read, not feeling lost but unsure what is next. A visitor recognizes their own situation.
- The illustration uses a small set of colors and many small details, so it is memorable and different from other sites.

## Where it is weak
- Text on the tilted cards is set at an angle, which slows reading.
- On a phone the hero shows only one card, and the illustrated scene is not visible in the first screens.

## The lesson
Use everyday questions on cards, set in an illustrated world, to show a visitor that their small worry is a fit for your service.

title: Warm people photos on a technical page
works: Serif headline on near-black hero
Audio card and answer grid show the product
Row of people photos makes it human
fixes: Phone view shows only part of the product
Headline is abstract for a business owner
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A technical product can look cold, and this page counters that with warm photographs of people on calls. The top is dark with a serif headline and one white button. A grey-lilac panel then shows a call recording next to a grid of questions and answers, so the product is explained as a picture.

## What works
- The serif type and restrained palette feel calm and careful.
- The audio card beside the answer grid shows what goes in and what comes out.
- The photo row of people on calls, with small cards for tone and context, links the tech to real life.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone, the product panel is cut off after the first card.
- The headline (audio-native decision model) is hard for a non-technical owner to understand.

## The lesson
Follow a dark technical hero with warm photos of real people, so the product feels human.

title: Full-photo hero with a torn-paper edge
works: Large photo of a person outdoors
Heavy headline says the offer in four words
Torn-paper edges give a distinct style
fixes: Some body text is pale on the sky
Phone hero crops the person away from text
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page uses a photo of a known person and a four-word headline to make a phone plan feel human. The brand style is easy to spot and the button is clear.

## What works
- A full-width photo of a person hugging a tree matches the headline about using your phone less.
- The heavy headline and the light blue button are easy to read at a glance.
- The torn-paper edges and the navy and sky blue palette make the page look different from other phone brands.

## Where it is weak
- Some body text sits in pale type on the cloud background and is hard to read.
- On the phone the text sits over the tree, so the photo and the words compete.

## The lesson
Choose a photo that acts out the headline, and give the page one visual device that only your brand uses.

title: A row of lifestyle photos for rent rewards
works: Plain headline: Get more out of your home
Tall photo cards show what points buy
Card offer sits in one clear strip
fixes: Lower laptop screen is empty
Body text is small and light grey
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A rent and mortgage rewards card is hard to picture, so the page shows what the points give: travel, dinners, fitness and shows. The row of tall photos moves the visitor from a dull bill to something they want.

## What works
- The headline is short and the paragraph under it names rent, mortgage and points in plain words.
- The photo cards are labelled Travel, Dining and Fitness, so each reward is clear at a glance.
- A single strip states the card offer, 1.25X points with no transaction fee, and has a small arrow to apply.

## Where it is weak
- The lower part of the laptop screen is empty white space after the offer strip.
- The body text and card descriptions are small and light grey.

## The lesson
Show what the reward feels like with real photos, and give the card offer its own clearly boxed line.

title: A coral block and big smiles feel friendly
works: Coral block with serif headline
Large real smile portraits
Clear free consultation button
fixes: Reviews use small, dense text
Treatment photos have no explanation
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Orthodontists often look clinical, and this page looks like a lifestyle brand. A large coral card holds a short headline and one button beside a smiling portrait. Big, real photos of patients run through the page.

## What works
- The headline, 'We straighten teeth well.', is short, in a serif face, on a coral block with a smile mark.
- The button 'Schedule a Free Consultation' is white on coral, with a second 'Start Virtual Consultation' tag on the photo.
- Three tall photo cards, for braces, aligners and the practice, give a visitor a way to choose a treatment.

## Where it is weak
- The review text is small and in long blocks, so a visitor will skip it.
- The three photo cards carry only a short label, so they say little about price, time or result.

## The lesson
Use one strong brand colour and big photos of real patients to make a clinical service feel friendly.

title: Dark hero over bright shop photos
works: Black hero with a calm two-tone headline
Row of colourful photos of real merch
Free-start line next to the button
fixes: Product grid is a common layout
Phone hero shows one image only
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A black hero with a light headline and one white button sits above a wide strip of vivid photos. The photos show real shops, a model in a shirt and a skateboarder, so the page feels like a brand and not a tool.

## What works
- The headline states the offer in two short lines, with the second line in grey.
- "No upfront costs. No credit card required." sits beside "Start now".
- The product section shows items with star ratings, which makes the catalog feel real.

## Where it is weak
- The product grid of uneven tiles is a familiar layout and adds little that is new.
- On the phone only one image of the strip is visible and the rest is cut off.

## The lesson
Put a strip of vivid real photos under a quiet headline so the colour comes from the work and not the page.

title: Serif headline over a glowing hero image
works: Large serif headline, one clear button
Dark and lime sections give strong contrast
Product shots sit in tidy cards
fixes: Hero image says little about the product
Phone first screen is mostly empty
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads

The page opens with one large serif headline and one button over a soft glowing image. The look is calm and unlike most finance sites. Dark and lime sections below keep the eye moving.

## What works

- The headline is big, short and easy to read. A single dark button gives the visitor one thing to press.
- The black and lime colours repeat in the buttons and cards, so the brand feels consistent.
- Cards with product screens show the trading tools without long text.

## Where it is weak

- The hero picture is abstract and does not show the product. On the phone view the space under the button is blank.
- Risk notices sit in small type near the top and pull attention from the offer.

## The lesson

Pair a bold serif headline with one button, but show the real product in the first screen.

title: Painted mountain scene softens a hard topic
works: Warm illustration replaces cold funeral stock photos
Serif headline mixes light and bold weights
Two clear buttons for urgent and planning needs
fixes: Review cards are small and hard to read
Phone view shows only a thin slice of art
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Funeral sites usually look heavy. After uses a warm painted landscape with a family on a hill, so the first screen feels calm and human. The two actions are easy to find.

## What works
- The illustration fills the first screen in warm peach, green and cream. It shows people living, not a building or flowers.
- The headline Funerals have a new home mixes light italic and bold serif type and states the change in four words.
- The orange button says A death has occurred, a plain phrase for someone in urgent need. A smaller link, or plan for the future, serves planners.

## Where it is weak
- The review cards use small italic grey text on pastel boxes, which is hard to read.
- On a phone the artwork shrinks to a narrow band and loses most of its effect.

## The lesson
For a sensitive service, use warm art and plain words, and give the urgent visitor one obvious button.

title: Italic serif headline beside a live price calculator
works: Headline promises honest weighing
Calculator and price strip show what you get
Four numbered steps explain the sale
fixes: Little imagery of real items or people
Five option links are small and quiet
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page sells honesty. The headline, Your gold, weighed honestly, uses an elegant serif with italics, and a live calculator beside it shows a price before the visitor gives any details.

## What works
- The headline and the line under it say what happens: tell us the carat and weight, we post a free insured pack, and we pay the same day you accept.
- A price strip lists what the shop pays per gram for 9ct, 14ct, 18ct, 22ct and a full sovereign. The visitor sees real numbers at once.
- A four-step block, numbered 01 to 04, explains the postal sale from estimate to same-day payment.

## Where it is weak
- The page has almost no photos of items, the shop or the team, so it feels bare.
- The five option links under What would you like to do are small and easy to miss.

## The lesson
Show the price a seller will get in the first screen and write the headline around a promise of fair treatment.

title: Studio finder inside a calm photo hero
works: Studio search box in the hero
Three cards sort visitors by their situation
Italic serif word in each headline
fixes: Two banners crowd the page top
Polished but fairly standard layout
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads

The headline "Pilates for everybody" sits over a strong photo, and the next thing a visitor sees is a box to find a local studio and a free intro class button. A calm cream and blue palette keeps the page easy on the eye.

## What works

- Three cards, The new arrival, Already a member and The returner, each have one matching button.
- A three-step How it works block, Book online, Arrive 15 min early, Your guided class, removes first-visit worries, with a question under each step.
- Figures for 1.5K studios, 21M+ classes and 19 years appear in large italic numerals.

## Where it is weak

- A top banner and a gift card banner both sit above the content, which crowds the first screen.
- The photo cards and numbers follow a common template that many gym sites use.

## The lesson

Sort visitors into three starting points with one button each, so every person sees a next step for them.

title: Mixed type weights and warm photo tiles
works: Headline mixes light grey and dark weights
Small photo tiles frame the hero text
Product screen sits on a warm background
fixes: Photos do not relate to customer service
Phone view is sparse with no product shown
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads

The headline puts the key words in dark type and the rest in light grey, so the eye lands on AI and human first. A free trial note under the buttons removes the cost worry.

## What works

- Two buttons, Start free trial and View demo, sit under the headline with a short line about the 14 day trial.
- The product screenshot shows a real inbox with a reply panel, so the visitor sees what the tool does.
- The review count above the headline gives early proof.

## Where it is weak

- The hero photos of a shadow, a sky and an eye do not explain the product.
- On the phone, the product screen is missing and a small chat bubble sits over the next section.

## The lesson

Use type weight to point to the key words, and show the real product under the buttons.

title: A task picker inside the hero
works: Tick boxes ask what the visitor wants to do
Photo with payroll cards shows the product
Review scores sit right under the button
fixes: Top offer bar and badge pile up near the hero
Card section below is a common layout
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads

The hero asks the visitor to choose a task, such as hire anywhere or run payroll, before pressing Book a demo. A photo of a person at a laptop with small payroll cards on it shows both the people and the product.

## What works

- The task boxes let the visitor say what they need in one tap.
- The photo has a payroll total, a visa approved tag and a customer quote on it.
- G2 and Trustpilot scores appear under the button, and the logo strip follows.

## Where it is weak

- The black offer bar, the purple expert pill and the logo strip all compete near the hero.
- The six product cards below are neat but look like many other software pages.

## The lesson

Let the visitor choose their goal in the hero, then show the product on a real photo.

title: Serif headline over a calm room photograph
works: Serif type feels premium, not technical
Product photographed as furniture on wood
Colour isometric drawing explains each room
fixes: Phone hero text crowds the photo
Cookie bar covers part of first screen
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page treats a heat pump like a piece of home design. A large photo of a calm room, a serif headline and a clean white button make a technical product feel desirable.

## What works
- The serif headline over a full-width photo gives the page a premium, calm tone.
- The indoor unit is shown on a wood wall with soft light, so it looks like furniture and not like machinery.
- An isometric drawing with room temperatures such as 72 and 68 degrees shows how room-by-room control works at a glance.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone, the headline and paragraph sit on top of the busy photo and are harder to read.
- The cookie banner covers the start of the next section on both screens.

## The lesson
Photograph a technical product in a real room so the buyer judges it as part of their home, not as equipment.

title: Square brackets frame every headline and image
works: Headline names search and AI results
Brackets repeat on every service card
Client logos and award badges build trust
fixes: Award badges are faint over the water
Paragraph text under cards is small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The headline says what the agency does in plain terms: front of mind, top of search and recommended in AI tools. A dark photo of water sits behind it. Large square brackets frame the headline, and the same brackets frame each service card. That one shape ties the whole page together.

## What works
- The headline names a clear result and mentions AI search, which many buyers now ask about.
- The four service cards use the same bracket frame, a photo, a few tags and a short paragraph, so they are easy to compare.
- A row of client logos, including Autotrader, M&S and Panasonic, sits right after the services.

## Where it is weak
- The award badges at the bottom of the first screen are faint and hard to read over the water.
- The paragraphs under the service cards are small, and the page has only a small Contact button to act on.

## The lesson
Pick one simple shape and repeat it on the headline and every card, so the page feels like one design.

title: A dreamy 3D world makes mortgages feel calm
works: Bold 3D scene sets a calm mood
Two clear buttons: buy or remortgage
Three numbered steps explain the service
fixes: Hero art can hide the headline
Phone view cuts off after first step
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Buying a home is stressful, and this page answers with a calm, colourful 3D world. The headline sits in a soft card over the scene, so the words stay easy to read. A visitor sees two buttons and picks the one that matches their situation.

## What works
- The hero headline, 'Home-buying made easier', is large and sits on a clear card over the artwork.
- Two buttons, 'I want to buy a home' and 'I want to remortgage', let a visitor choose a path at once.
- The page explains the service in three numbered cards, each with its own illustration and a short plain line.

## Where it is weak
- The busy 3D background competes with the text, and a viewer may look at the art before the offer.
- On the phone, the first screen shows the headline and buttons, but the next card is cut off, so the steps are not visible without scrolling.

## The lesson
Put a big plain headline on a solid card over bold artwork, so the mood is memorable and the offer stays readable.

title: Cutout children in a row, grid below
works: Cutout photo of many children
Thin grid lines with color blocks
Three short reasons with photos
fixes: Row text is small
Phone view has much empty space
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The top of the page is a row of children cut out against white, each doing something different, such as tug of war, skipping rope or wearing a space helmet. It is lively without needing a background. Below, a thin grid with a few blocks of blue, yellow, orange and green gives the page a clear structure.

## What works
- The cutout row of children is memorable and shows a range of kids at once.
- The heading "School for what's ahead" and a single Find a school button give one clear step.
- Three rows, Fundamentals-Focused, Safe Caring Classrooms and Truly Accessible, each have a short line and a small photo.

## Where it is weak
- The text in the three rows is small and sits far from the titles, so the rows are slow to read.
- On the phone, the grid lines leave a lot of empty space around the headline.

## The lesson
Build the page on a visible grid with a few blocks of color, and let one lively photo of real people set the mood.

title: Watercolour hero behind a tight stack of service cards
works: Oversized dark headline stands out against the watercolour
Indigo palette and bottle renders feel consistent throughout
Trust strip with Trustpilot score sits right under the hero
fixes: Hero holds too many cards and links
Trust strip is cut off at the edges

## What works
- The heavy, tightly set headline in dark indigo is easy to read over the blue and violet watercolour. It gives the page a clear voice that looks different from a typical clinic site.
- One indigo colour is used for the buttons, tags, product renders and the dark band lower down. This keeps the page consistent and makes the buttons easy to spot.
- The page uses a real clinician with her name and title, along with phone screens showing the care plan. This shows what the service is, not only what it sells.

## Where it is weak
- The hero shows two large cards and four small link cards, plus a rating and a button. The visitor has many choices at once, and the two large cards compete with the main button.
- The trust strip runs off the edge of the screen, so some text

title: Dark cinematic street photography with prices
works: Street scene photos make the cars feel real
Starting prices show on each model card
Dark page with serif headings looks premium
fixes: Layout follows a familiar car site pattern
Top offer banner text is long and small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page is dark, with photos of two cars on city streets at dusk. A white "Get early access" button sits under a Black Friday offer. Below, each model has a starting price and two buttons. A visitor can compare cars, see the price and act.

## What works
- The hero photo puts the car in a real street with people walking by. It feels like a place, not a studio.
- Model cards show "Starting at $70,900" and "$79,900" with "Design yours" and "Explore" side by side.
- The section "More of what matters" uses tall photo cards with a short label, such as Fast and Easy Charging, for the questions buyers have.

## Where it is weak
- The structure of hero, model cards and carousel is common to many car brands.
- The banner at the top carries a long lease offer in very small type, and it wraps over three lines on a phone.

## The lesson
Put the starting price and both actions, one to build and one to learn more, on every model card.

title: Light serif headline over a live data table
works: Light serif headline with one bold phrase
Hero shows a real table of companies
Sharp buttons and a clear trusted-by strip
fixes: A large black block is empty
Phone hero crops the product screen
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Twenty is a CRM for technical teams that want to build their own. The page looks like a well-made tool rather than a sales brochure. A thin serif headline with bold emphasis, black buttons with cut corners and a table that looks like the real product all say this is for people who build things. A strip of customer logos sits just under the table.

## What works
- The headline, "Build your Enterprise CRM at AI Speed", is large and centred, with two plain buttons below it.
- The product screen is a real companies table with a floating AI chat box. It shows what you get right away.
- The Problem section contrasts two bad choices, a giant monolith and an in-house build, in two short blocks.

## Where it is weak
- A big black rectangle beside the Problem heading has nothing in it. It looks like a missing picture.
- On a phone, the product table is cut off at the right edge and the first screen shows only part of it.

## The lesson
If your buyers are technical, show the real product table in the hero and let the type and buttons look like a tool they would respect.

title: Close-up of laughing children as the hero
works: Emotive photo fills the first screen
Serif headline with one bright button
Reviews and awards sit directly below
fixes: Layout follows a common fintech pattern
Review cards leave large empty space
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Two laughing children fill the first screen and the headline "Protect the life you've built" ties the photo to the purchase. A bright green Check my price button and a review score sit within reach. The page asks for little commitment.

## What works
- The photo carries the emotion, so the headline can stay short.
- One bright button, Check my price, stands out clearly against the dark photo.
- Trustpilot and Google ratings, awards and a quoted customer follow straight after the first screen.

## Where it is weak
- The section order and card style are what most financial sites use.
- The review cards hold short quotes with a lot of empty space.

## The lesson
Let one strong photo carry the emotion and keep the button the brightest thing on the screen.

- Insurance logos (Health Net, UnitedHealthcare, Cigna, Aetna) and a Check your coverage button answer the cost question. A short note says coverage depends on the plan.

- The small light text on the blue clinician section is thin and hard to read. The quote card there also covers part of the photo.
- On the phone, the hero photo is cropped to one face and the care plan cards shrink to very small labels.

## The lesson
Pair one oversized headline with a real photo, then show a concrete exa

title: Ask box surrounded by attorney portraits
works: Text box invites a question straight away
Tappable example questions sit under the box
Faces of attorneys make the help feel human
fixes: Headline grey and soft against the white
Phone view pushes the faces above the box
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The first screen puts a large ask box in the middle, ringed by photos of attorneys. A visitor can type a legal question at once or tap an example. The photos show that real people stand behind the tool.

## What works
- The ask box is the main action, so the visitor starts without reading anything.
- Three example questions show what to type, which helps a visitor who is unsure.
- A grid of attorney portraits gives a human face to the service.

## Where it is weak
- The headline is a soft grey and has less contrast than the rest of the page.
- On a phone the portraits take the first screen and the ask box moves down.

## The lesson
Put the first step on the page itself as a box the visitor can use, and show the people behind it.

title: Dark product screen as the whole first view
works: Short headline in large white type
Real product screen with live activity
Customer logos in one clean row
fixes: Grey text on black is hard to read
Phone view crops the product screen
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page is nearly all black and grey, with large white type and one big product screen. There are no photos. The product itself is the picture, and the page keeps a strict, calm style.

## What works
- The headline "The product development system for teams and agents" is large and uses two short lines on desktop.
- The product screen shows an issue, a chat with an agent and an activity list, so a visitor sees the tool at work.
- A row of logos from OpenAI, Vercel, Figma and others appears right after the screen.

## Where it is weak
- Body text and labels are dark grey on black, and the contrast is low.
- On the phone the product screen runs off the right edge, so the visitor sees only part of it.

## The lesson
Make the real product screen the hero picture and keep all other styling quiet.

title: Bold black hero with product screens collage
works: Offer and price sit in the hero text
Screens and real people show the product
Trust badges sit right under the hero
fixes: Green announcement bar repeats the offer
Two stacked menus crowd the top
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens on black with a large white headline, a line that states the offer, 3 months free then from 14 pounds a month, and one green button. A collage of invoices, a dashboard and photos of small business owners shows the product and the buyer. A visitor knows the price and the action before scrolling.

## What works
- The offer and the monthly price sit in the hero text, so the visitor does not hunt for cost.
- The collage mixes real product screens with photos of owners, so the software feels made for them.
- Trustpilot, HMRC recognised and Making Tax Digital ready sit directly under the hero, where doubt is highest.

## Where it is weak
- A green announcement bar and two menu bars stack above the headline and push it down.
- The same free offer shows in the bar, the top button and the hero button, which adds noise.

## The lesson
Put the price and the free offer in the hero text, then place your trust badges directly beneath it.

title: Pink button on deep purple, savings upfront
works: Headline states the saving in pounds
Pink Get a quote button stands out
Price cards give average costs by cover
fixes: Rewards banner competes with the main button
Small footnote marks clutter the text
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens on deep purple with a headline that promises a saving of up to 563 pounds. One bright pink button, Get a quote, is the only strong colour. A strip of three ticks and a Trustpilot score sit right below it.

## What works
- The headline gives a number the visitor cares about, and the pink button is the one action on screen.
- The three cover types sit in cards with plain explanations, so a first-time buyer can choose.
- Average prices for each cover type appear in large figures, which helps a visitor judge a quote.

## Where it is weak
- The SuperSaveClub rewards panel with large coins sits close to the button and pulls the eye.
- Many small footnote numbers sit in headlines and prices and make the text feel busy.

## The lesson
Lead with a real money figure in the headline and keep one bright button as the only loud colour.

title: Quote box that asks your business type
works: Quote box asks one easy question
Four cover cards show starting prices
Colourful portraits give the brand a face
fixes: Large blank gap beside the intro text
Fund and campaigns sections distract from quotes
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens on a strong purple field with a short headline and a quote box that asks one question: what type of business do you want to insure. Below it, four cards show the cover types with starting prices. A visitor can start a quote in one step.

## What works
- The quote box asks one plain question with examples like builder, cleaner and restaurant, so starting is easy.
- Four cards for public liability, professional indemnity, employers liability and landlord cover show a from price.
- Insurer logos and a Feefo rating sit just under the hero and build trust before the visitor scrolls.

## Where it is weak
- A large blank area sits beside the Helping to protect your small business text, which looks like a missing image.
- The Win 10k and Research sections move attention away from getting a quote.

## The lesson
Put a one-question quote box in the hero and show a from price on each cover type.

title: Room photos sell every sofa in the grid
works: Every product photo shows a styled room
Price, rating and discount on each card
Filters sit above the product grid
fixes: Sale banner colour clashes with the pink
Long list of filters crowds the top
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
This is a category page, so the job is to help a buyer pick a sofa fast. Each card shows the sofa in a real room, with the price, the star rating and the discount in the same place. A shopper can compare 12 sofas in one scroll.

## What works
- Photos show each sofa in a lived-in room, which helps a buyer see it in their own home.
- Every card repeats the same four facts: name, price, rating with review count, and discount tag.
- Trust items (finance, points, 100,000+ reviews) sit in a thin strip above the heading.

## Where it is weak
- Eleven filter buttons and a two-row menu push the first sofa below the fold on a laptop.
- The red sale bar, pink tags and red prices compete for attention.

## The lesson
Give every product card the same four facts in the same spot, and show the product in use, not on white.

title: Condensed headline in navy and green over real roof photos
works: Big condensed headline states the promise at once
Navy, green and yellow palette stays consistent
Real before and after photos show the result
fixes: Hero photo card overlaps the text and looks glitchy
Section layouts feel like a stock template
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens with a promise a homeowner understands in one look: never clean your gutters again, for life. The yellow button stands out against the pale background and is repeated further down. Real photos of a roof edge and of pine needles in a gutter back up the claim.

## What works
- The tall condensed headline is large and easy to read. Its last line turns green to stress the promise "Again. For life."
- The palette is limited to navy, green and yellow, with yellow kept for buttons and labels. This makes the next step easy to spot on both laptop and phone.
- The before and after photo in the green panel shows clogged pine needles next to a clean roof edge. A line below it states the lifetime guarantee, and a button sits beside it.

## Where it is weak
- In the hero, the small photo card overlaps the large photo and the sections beneath it, and a dark navy bar cuts across the content. It looks like a rendering error.
- The block layouts (rounded colored panels, a headline on the left and a graphic on the right) look like a common template. The Greenville panel has little that is specific to this company.

## The lesson
Put one plain, bold promise in

title: One product on a calm grey gradient
works: Single lock photo gives one clear focus
Numbered benefit list is easy to scan
Book a demo button stays in view
fixes: Benefit descriptions are very small text
Headline says the category, not the benefit
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page shows one product, a black smart lock, on a soft grey gradient with a large plain headline and one Book a demo button. Nothing else competes for attention at the top. A property manager sees what the product is and what to do next.

## What works
- The hero has one lock, one headline and one button. The eye goes straight to the action.
- The five numbered benefits sit in a ruled list with short titles, so a manager can scan them in seconds.
- The Book a demo button appears in the top bar and in the hero, so it is always close.

## Where it is weak
- The text beside each benefit is small and grey, and hard to read on a laptop.
- The headline, Residential Doors, names the page and does not say what the buyer gains.

## The lesson
Give a product page one hero object and one button, then list the benefits in a short numbered table.

title: Big serif headline over a pack shot
works: Lime offer bar says the discount at once
Pack photo labels protein, fibre, carbs
Four-step row shows how ordering works
fixes: Two Find out more buttons lead away
Press logos are grey and low contrast
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The top of the page has a lime bar with the discount, a large serif headline, Trustpilot stars and one Get offer button. A photo of three meals in dark green sleeves fills the right side. The colours are few and the page looks like a food brand.

## What works
- The offer bar says 40% off week one and 15% off weeks two and three. The same words appear in the button.
- The pack photo has small labels pointing to high protein, high fibre and low carb.
- Four photos in a row, from choosing meals to feeling the benefits, explain the service with no reading.

## Where it is weak
- Find out more buttons sit mid page and send visitors off the offer.
- The press logos are grey and thin, so they add little proof.

## The lesson
Put the discount in a bar and in the button text, and label the product photo with the facts a buyer checks.

title: Body part and postcode box starts the booking
works: Booking bar with body part and location
Four ticks answer the first questions
Patient reviews appear with names and photos
fixes: Chat button overlaps the page on the phone
Intro paragraph is small and dense
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A person who needs a scan wants to know what it covers, whether they need a referral, and where to go. The page answers with four ticks (no GP referral required is one), then a booking bar that asks for the body part and a postcode. A photo of a real scanner room with a smiling patient makes the visit feel less scary.

## What works
- A short booking bar with Body Parts, Location and a pink Book button sits on the first screen.
- Four ticks, such as No GP referral required, answer common worries in a few words.
- Three patient reviews with names, photos and stars follow a dark banner that offers a £50 consultation call.

## Where it is weak
- The chat button sits over the page edge on both laptop and phone.
- The paragraph under the heading is small and full of long phrases.

## The lesson
Put a two-field booking bar on the first screen and use ticks to answer the buyer's biggest worries before they scroll.

title: Heritage polaroids and tall condensed type
works: Tall condensed headlines are easy to read
Real crew photos show actual workers on a roof
Orange buttons stand out against dark photos
fixes: Hero body text is small over a busy photo
Chat widget and prompt cover the phone hero
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads

The page opens with a plain headline, "Commercial Roofing Contractor," over a photo of workers in hard hats and safety vests on a flat roof. It then backs up its age claim with old photographs and a sign that states the company's work standard. A visitor can see that this is a long-established firm with real people. The orange button and the phone number stay in view at every step.

## What works

- The tall condensed type is bold and consistent. Headlines like "Over 100 Years" and "We shall do good work" can be read quickly and give the page a clear voice.
- The scattered black-and-white polaroids next to the "Serving businesses for over 100 years" line show the company's age instead of only stating it. The orange arrow and orange words draw the eye along the line.
- The orange is used sparingly, on the small label, the buttons and the phone alert icon. The next step is easy to spot on both desktop and phone. The phone number and urgent service link sit in the top bar.

## Where it is weak

- The hero paragraph is small and thin over a photo with a lot of detail, so it is hard to read. The small orange label above the headline also gets lost on the phon

title: Identical tubs make the grid easy to scan
works: Same pack style on every product
Sale price shown next to the old price
Green cart button on each product photo
fixes: Intro text is cut off by a fade
Red discount lines under each price are small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The products share one look, a black tub with a white label, so the eye moves from card to card and reads only the names and prices. The cart button sits on the photo, so a buyer can add an item without opening it. The page behaves like a shelf in a shop.

## What works
- Every card follows the same order: photo, name, size, stars, price and offer.
- The old price is crossed out beside the new price, which makes the saving clear.
- The round green cart button on each photo gives one clear action.

## Where it is weak
- The category intro is cut off and fades out, so a visitor cannot read why magnesium matters.
- The red offer line under each price is small and repeats the same code.

## The lesson
Give every product card the same layout and put the add-to-cart button on the photo so buying takes one click.

title: Cruise search form sits at the top
works: Phone view opens with a cruise search form
Three benefits shown under the form
Large ship and beach photo in the hero
fixes: Laptop capture shows no page styling
Phone chat bubble covers the headline
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
On the phone, the first thing a visitor sees is a search form with where from, where to, when, how long and who is going. Under it, three short benefits (all-inclusive, low deposits, Trustpilot rating) give reasons to book. The task is clear from the first screen.

## What works
- The phone screen opens with a search form, so a visitor can start a booking at once.
- Three icons under the form state all-inclusive, deposits from £125pp and a review rating.
- The laptop capture shows a wide photo of a ship at a beach, which sells the trip.

## Where it is weak
- The laptop capture shows plain text and links with no styling, so the grader's picture of the laptop page is unreliable.
- A chat bubble covers the headline on the phone.

## The lesson
Start the page with a search form that matches the buyer's task, and place two or three plain benefits right under it.

title: Warm lowercase serif with friendly icons
works: Lowercase serif gives a warm, gentle voice
Three cards explain the services simply
Three numbered steps show how to book
fixes: Hero is a flat block with no photo
Call to Book repeats with no other options
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page feels like a friendly neighbourhood clinic. It uses a lowercase serif, a cream background and a soft green hero, and the tone stays calm for an owner worried about a pet. Short sections explain the services and the booking steps.

## What works
- The lowercase serif headings and rounded cards give the page a warm, kind voice.
- Three service cards with simple icons explain what the clinic treats in a few words each.
- A three step How to book section shows what happens at the first visit, which removes doubt.

## Where it is weak
- The hero is a plain green block with no photo of a pet or a vet, so it feels empty.
- Every button says Call to Book, and there is no online option beside it.

## The lesson
Explain the first visit in three numbered steps, in a warm voice, so an anxious owner knows what to expect.

title: Full-bleed kitchen photo, quiet neutral layout
works: Full-width kitchen photo fills the first screen
Calm beige palette matches the work shown
Material samples show the design approach
fixes: No call to action in the first screen
Small menu text is hard to read
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page opens with a large kitchen image and nothing else competing with it. The colours on the page match the colours in the rooms, so the site itself looks like the firm's work. A visitor who likes the look keeps scrolling to see more.

## What works
- The first screen is one full-width kitchen image with the logo centred above it. The quality of the work is clear straight away.
- The beige background, soft grey text and wood tones repeat the palette of the photos. The page feels like one designed space.
- A split section pairs a short statement with a photo of material samples. It shows how the firm works, not only the end result.

## Where it is weak
- The first screen has no button or contact option. A visitor ready to enquire must look for the menu.
- The menu text is small and light. On the phone, the first screen shows only the logo, a cart count and a menu icon.

## The lesson
Let one large photo carry the first screen and match the page colours to it, but add one clear enquiry button on top of that photo.

title: Close skin photography with a blunt headline
works: Large close-up photo sets a mood
Plain headline says what the studio does
Service rows use photo, name and one line
fixes: Photo crop may feel too close for some
Booking notice banner crowds the phone top
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page uses a large, tightly cropped photo and a short, plain headline. It reads as a studio with a point of view, not a generic spa. The service list under the intro shows each treatment as a wide photo row with a name and one line, so a visitor can pick fast.

## What works
- The first screen is one big close-up photo with a short white headline across the bottom. The mood is clear with no extra elements.
- The headline "Massage therapy & bodywork built for real life" says the service and the audience's need in one line. The location line sits just above it.
- The treatment rows each have a photo, a name, one sentence and a "Get the details" link. Names such as "Profound" and "Engine Room" hint at who each one suits.

## Where it is weak
- The tight crop hides the face and may feel too intense for a first-time visitor who wants to see the room or the therapist.
- A purple booking-system notice sits above the header, and on the phone it takes a large block of the first screen.

## The lesson
Use one strong photo and one plain sentence in the first screen, then list services as photo rows with a single line each.

title: Full-bleed portrait of the teacher
works: Portrait of the teacher fills the screen
Serif title is large and quiet
Price sits on the button
fixes: Buttons are small and pale on phone
Email bar covers part of hero
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The course opens with one large portrait of the teacher and the course title in serif type. The price is on the Add to cart button, so the buyer knows the cost at once.

## What works
- The photo is the teacher's own work and sets the tone for the course.
- The title, gift button and cart button sit together at the bottom of the image.
- Three short facts, 19 lessons, 5+ hours and 24/7 access, sit in a plain row below.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone, the buttons are thin and small over a busy photo.
- A black email bar sits under the hero and uses space.

## The lesson
Lead a course page with a strong image of the teacher and put the price on the buy button.

title: House-shaped photo crops and an italic promise
works: Photos cut into house shapes
Italic line: we sell to someone
Search box right under the hero
fixes: Hero has no contact button on phone
Small grey labels in the search form
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page has a clear idea and shows it. Four interior photos are cut into house outlines, and one line below says other agents sell to anyone while this one sells to someone. The green and cream palette is the same all the way down.

## What works
- The house-shaped photo crops turn a plain row of images into a memorable brand shape.
- The italic serif line sets the company apart from other agents in a few words.
- A listing search sits on the first screen, with the latest listings and prices below.

## Where it is weak
- On a phone the first screen has no appraisal or contact button, only the search form.
- The District and Suburb labels in the search are pale grey and hard to read.

## The lesson
Turn one photo shape and one sharp line into the brand, and keep the same colours across the page.

title: Calm serif type sells one-team renovation
works: Large bathroom photo sets a calm tone
Serif headline with italic second half
Section explains why gaps between trades hurt
fixes: No reviews or numbers in the first screens
Intro text over the photo is small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page feels like a design studio, not a builder. A finished bathroom photo, a refined serif headline and wide spacing suggest care. The copy then names the real fear in a renovation, which is trades not working together.

## What works
- The hero photo shows a finished bathroom with tiles, mirrors and a vanity. The headline sits over it in cream serif type, with an italic second half.
- "One project, not a string of tradespeople" names the buyer's worry in six words and answers it.
- A tidy two-column list shows what is included, from consultation to final clean. The phone view keeps call and book buttons fixed at the bottom.

## Where it is weak
- The first screens show no review score, past clients or numbers, so trust is left for later.
- The small paragraph in the hero is hard to read over the photo.

## The lesson
Name the biggest fear of your buyer in the headline of the first section, then show how your process removes it.

title: Moody studio photography makes flowers feel like art
works: Dark, painterly hero photo sets the mood
Hero states same-day delivery and cut-off time
Bouquets shown held by a person
fixes: Small, light type is hard to read
Product grid below hero looks repetitive
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page sells a feeling before it sells a product. A large, dark, painterly photo of a wild arrangement fills the first screen, and the headline states the service plainly: same-day flower delivery in Los Angeles. A visitor knows what is sold, where, and how fast within a few seconds.

## What works
- The hero photo has a calm, moody look that makes the flowers feel handmade and unusual.
- The hero names the city, the delivery promise and the order cut-off time in two short lines.
- Product photos show each bouquet held by a person against the same grey backdrop, so the grid feels like one set.

## Where it is weak
- Body text and labels are small and thin, and some sit low in contrast on the beige background.
- The product grid repeats one photo style with similar names, so it is hard to tell the choices apart.

## The lesson
Lead with one strong photo style and a plain delivery promise, then repeat that photo style across every product.

title: Two quote cards inside the first screen
works: Instant and on-site quote cards sit in hero
Bold green headline names service and area
Review score and checks sit under the text
fixes: Many styles compete in the first screen
Phone first screen shows no call button
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The first screen lets a visitor start a quote without leaving it. Two large cards offer an instant quote in about 60 seconds or a free on-site visit. The headline names the service and the area, and the page looks like a local business, not a template.

## What works
- The two quote cards give a choice of effort. The orange card is the fast route and the green card is the visit route.
- The headline "Lawn mowing in Melbourne's north, done properly" is large and heavy, with a green highlight on the last words. The service and place are clear.
- A 4.9 Google score with 70+ reviews, plus "Police checked" and "Fully insured" badges, sit right under the intro text. Trust is visible at once.

## Where it is weak
- The tilted photo, speech bubble, stickers and price tag add many styles in one area, and the eye has no single place to start.
- On the phone, the top bar shows a chat icon and a menu icon but no call or quote button, so the cards carry all the action.

## The lesson
Put the quote step itself in the first screen as two clear options, and show review proof directly beside it.

title: Neon green brand with a character hero
works: Neon green fills every section and hero
Headline rejects the usual wallet idea
Phone view keeps headline, photo and button
fixes: Hero photo may confuse some visitors
Statistics strip is cut off at the edges
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page uses one loud neon green and heavy black type, so it looks like no other finance app. The headline says the product is not just another wallet, and the first screen has a single app download button. The phone view keeps the same bold look with the photo and button in view.

## What works
- One neon green colour fills the hero, the strip and the sections. The brand is recognised in a second.
- The hero has a clear claim, one line of benefits and one black button. A visitor knows what to do next.
- Product screens and object photos, such as the account card and the plant pot, explain growth and savings without long text.

## Where it is weak
- The hero man with a card is odd and gives no sign of what the app does until the text is read.
- The statistics strip is cut off at the edge, so the numbers are hard to read.

## The lesson
Pick one saturated brand colour and use it on every section, so the page is remembered before anyone reads it.

title: Black and white photo with a yellow burst
works: Tall condensed headline in white on dark teal
Yellow sun shape behind the two women
Two round yellow buttons with clear labels
fixes: Headline is a slogan, not an offer
No price or saving shown on the first screen
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero uses a black and white photo of two business women, a yellow circle behind them and short lines radiating out. It looks different from other energy supplier pages. The yellow buttons stand out against the dark teal.

## What works
- The tall condensed headline "Resilience is brilliance" is large and easy to read in white on teal.
- The yellow shape and lines give the photo energy without adding extra text.
- Two buttons, "Explore solar" and "Switch supply", split the visitor into two clear paths.

## Where it is weak
- The headline is a slogan. It does not say what the visitor saves or gets.
- No price, saving or proof appears on the first screen.

## The lesson
Pick one colour as the accent, use it for the photo shape and the buttons, and then add a plain line that says what the buyer gets.

title: Hand-drawn beach scene with pets on every section
works: Drawn pets make the brand easy to recall
Serif headline feels calm and trusted
Red button repeats on every section
fixes: Phone hero cuts off the drawing
Coverage text is dense below the fold
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Insurance pages usually look alike. This one has a drawn beach scene with a cat building a sand castle and a dog hang gliding. The pets in the drawings turn the headline, adventures together, into a picture.

## What works
- The line drawings are a style no competitor can copy easily. They return as a cat on a sand castle and a cat on a flamingo float in later sections.
- The headline is a large dark blue serif on a pale blue background. It reads as warm and steady, which suits a product about care.
- A red button with the same label, Explore our coverage, appears in the hero and again at the end of the page.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone the drawing is cropped to a strip, so the scene loses most of its charm.
- The coverage section is a long list of checks and a block of small text. It is harder to scan than the hero.

## The lesson
Commission one drawing style for your product, repeat its characters on each section, and use a calm serif headline to set the tone.

title: Styled cat photo on deep green
works: Cat, tins and ferns styled as one scene
Serif headline and one pale blue button
Trial price shown on a round badge
fixes: Cookie box covers part of the hero
Only the first screen is shown here
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero is a single styled photo, a cat licking its lips beside stacked tins on stone, on deep green. A serif headline and one pale button say what the food is and how to try it. The trial price sits on a round badge.

## What works
- The photo is staged like a magazine shot, so the tins look like a premium product and the cat looks keen.
- The green background, cream type and blue button use few colours, and the button stands out.
- A star rating, a meals delivered count and press names sit close to the headline, so the proof is early.

## Where it is weak
- A cookie box sits over the lower right of the hero on the laptop and over the phone screen.
- The card shows little beyond the hero, so the rest of the page is not shown to judge.

## The lesson
Stage the product with the pet in one photo, and put the trial price on a badge next to it.

title: Packaging shot sets a calm, premium tone
works: Packaging photo makes quitting look desirable
Serif type and green palette stay calm
Plain headline: Ditch vaping, then one button
fixes: Press logos sit before any proof
Two nav buttons compete with the main one
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page treats quitting like a lifestyle product, not a medical chore. The first screen shows colourful boxes and tins on a soft green background, so a visitor sees a brand they might be proud to carry. The headline is short and direct, and one button sits under it.

## What works
- The hero photo shows the full product range in matching colours. It is clear what you get and it looks good.
- The serif headline and muted green background feel calm. This suits people who feel stressed about quitting.
- The headline names the habit: "Ditch vaping." On phone it changes to "Ditch pouches." The visitor sees their own problem at once.

## Where it is weak
- The press logo strip comes right after the hero but gives no quote or detail, so it adds little proof.
- The nav has a "Find your plan" button next to "Shop the mints". Two paths split attention on the first screen.

## The lesson
Show the product in one styled photo that makes the change look attractive, then put one plain headline and one button next to it.

title: Warm photo hero with torn-paper edge
works: Photo shows a person and pig together
Hand-drawn pig marks each section
Torn edges and warm browns feel handmade
fixes: Hero text is small over a busy photo
Support Us button is small in the menu
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero is a real photo of a woman kneeling with a pig and a dog. The headline Our Mission is Kindness sits over it. The torn-paper edge, brown tones and hand-drawn pig give the page a warm voice that matches the cause.

## What works
- The photo shows care between a person and an animal, which says the mission without more words.
- Small line drawings of a pig and a hen link the sections and give the brand its own look.
- Torn-paper edges and a brown story card feel handmade, and the phone view keeps the same style.

## Where it is weak
- The short paragraph under the headline is small and sits over a busy part of the photo.
- The pink Support Us button is small and sits in the menu, with no large giving button in the hero.

## The lesson
Use one honest photo of the people and animals you help, and add a hand-made detail that only your brand would have.

title: Warm hero photo with live sale bundle
works: Warm sunset photo makes the product desirable
Trust strip shows warranty, shipping, customer count
Quiz helps shoppers pick a product
fixes: Phone view opens covered by an email popup
Hero text over photo is small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page mixes a calm, aspirational photo with a plain shop below it. A woman rests in a cold plunge at golden hour, a Black Friday offer sits in the bottom left, and a bundle card gives a quick way to buy.

## What works
- The "$2,500 off" headline is placed over the photo, so the sale and the product appear together.
- A strip under the hero lists a five-year warranty, free shipping, California build and 8,000+ customers. Those answer the main doubts early.
- A short quiz, "What are you after?", offers three buttons and reveals a match, which helps people who do not know which product to pick.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone, an email sign-up box covers the hero at once, before the visitor sees the offer.
- The line under the headline and the bundle card text are small and sit on a busy photo.

## The lesson

The hero uses leaf-shaped photo crops in teal, orange and cream beside a plain headline. Right under it, a search box asks for city, state or ZIP. The shapes make the page look unlike a clinic site, while the price in the text answers the main worry.

## What works
- The petal shapes tie the photo, the colours and the logo into one idea.
- The line "$40-70 per session, plus a one-time membership fee" gives the price straight away.
- The search box turns the first click into a real task: finding a therapist near you.

## Where it is weak
- The "Message Open Path" chat bar sits on top of the next section heading.
- On the phone the search box slips to the top edge and the big shapes take most of the screen.

## The lesson
Use one unusual image shape, but keep the price and the first action in plain text beside it.

title: A yellow highlight makes the headline unforgettable
works: Yellow highlight marks key headline words
Real crew photo builds trust
Hero says no deposit, no sales calls
fixes: Header links are small and crowded
Lower page is text heavy
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
Moving companies often look alike. This page uses one yellow highlight and a real photo of its crew to look different. The hero tells the visitor what to do and what will not happen: no deposit and no sales call.

## What works
- The headline, 'Dallas, meet your buddies', has yellow marker shapes behind key words, and the same yellow repeats through the page.
- A real photo of the crew by the truck, with a yellow offset frame, shows who will arrive at the door.
- The line under the headline and the note under the button, 'Takes about a minute', remove two common worries.

## Where it is weak
- The top bar holds many links and a phone number in small type, so it is busy next to the clean hero.
- The lower sections use small grey body text in six blocks, which is harder to scan than the hero.

## The lesson
Choose one bold brand colour, use it as a highlight on the headline, and pair it with a real photo of your own team.

title: Give form placed on a smiling portrait
works: Donation form sits in the hero
Smiling photo shows the result of giving
Serif headline is calm and clear
fixes: Cookie banner covers the hero
Phone hero has no form, only a button
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A large photo of a child drinking water fills the hero, and a small donation form sits on top of it. A visitor can choose an amount without leaving the first screen.

## What works
- The monthly and one-time tabs, preset amounts and one yellow button make giving fast.
- A single close-up photo shows the outcome of a gift.
- The serif headline is short and sits on a plain teal sky.

## Where it is weak
- A privacy banner covers the lower part of the hero on both laptop and phone.
- On the phone, the form is replaced by a Give today button.

## The lesson
Put the main action, with preset choices, directly on a photo that shows the result.

title: Three colour-coded service cards under a photo hero
works: Full-width playground photo shows the product
Stats bar: 1997, 4.8 stars, 430 videos
Green, blue and red cards split the services
fixes: Small white text on busy photo
Phone stats row is cut off
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The first screen shows a finished playground surface, says who the company is in one line, and gives two ways to act: a quote button and a phone number. A stats bar right below the photo adds proof before the visitor scrolls.

## What works
- The hero photo is the real product, a coloured rubber surface under a slide. A school buyer sees the result at once.
- The stats bar gives the year 1997, 184 case studies, a 4.8 Google rating and accreditation badges in one row.
- Three cards in green, blue and red separate playground, sports and resin work. Each card has a photo, a short line and tags.

## Where it is weak
- The small body text sits on a busy photo, so it is hard to read.
- On the phone, the stats row is cut off at the bottom of the first screen.

## The lesson
Put a proof bar directly under the hero photo, then give each service its own colour so the visitor picks a path fast.

title: Live-camera promise in a rich green and gold hero
works: Headline promises live camera views
Gold button and phone number side by side
Six included features in simple cards
fixes: Logo is busy over the photo
Hero holds too many small items
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page leads with the one thing a worried pet owner wants: to watch their pet live. The headline says so, and a gold Book holiday boarding button sits beside a call button. Dark green and gold colours feel warm and trusted.

## What works
- The headline, Holiday boarding where you can watch them live, names a clear benefit in a serif type that feels premium.
- A gold booking button and a phone number sit side by side, and on the phone a fixed bar adds Call, Text and Book.
- Six small cards list what is included, such as live camera, private suites and medications, so there are no hidden costs.

## Where it is weak
- The logo is detailed and sits on a busy photo, so it is hard to read.
- The hero stacks a banner, a tag, badges, links and ratings, which is a lot above the fold.

## The lesson
Lead with the single reassurance your buyer worries about, and give them a call and a book button together.

title: Dark cinematic photos with restrained serif type
works: Large dark photo of a finished pool
Thin light type on black feels premium
Named projects shown as big photos
fixes: No clear action on first screen
Phone text sits over a busy photo
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page sells luxury through its photos. A dark reflective pool and a house in the first screen signal high-end work. Project names set in thin serif type beside large images let the work speak.

## What works
- The first screen is a single large photo with one short paragraph, so nothing competes with the pool.
- The project section uses a black panel with a name and tall photos, which looks like a gallery.
- The type is thin and light with wide spacing, which matches the premium tone.

## Where it is weak
- The first screen has no button for a quote or a call. The only link is "Watch our showreel".
- On a phone the paragraph sits over a busy photo and is harder to read.

## The lesson
Use big project photos to signal quality, and add one visible enquiry link so a keen buyer can act.

title: Peach and navy brand with a sticky phone bar
works: Peach and navy palette is distinct
Navy Reserve tab stays at the top
Phone view has Menu, Call, Reserve bar
fixes: Hero text is plain over the cocktail
Body text is small on peach
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page uses a peach and navy palette with a hand-drawn line pattern, so it looks like no other restaurant site. A navy Reserve A Table tab hangs from the header on the laptop. On a phone, a fixed bar at the bottom offers Menu, Call and Reserve.

## What works
- The peach, navy and copper colours repeat in the header, the pattern panel and the navy band. The brand feels complete.
- The Reserve tab sits in the header and the phone bar stays at the bottom. Booking is always one tap away.
- Hours of operation sit beside the story text. A diner can plan a visit without leaving the page.

## Where it is weak
- The hero text and logo mark sit over a dark cocktail photo and look thin and crowded together.
- The story and hours text is small and set in a light tone on the peach background.

## The lesson
Give the phone a fixed bottom bar with Call and Reserve, and carry one distinct two-colour brand through every section.

title: Serif headline over a real storage corridor
works: Real corridor photo shows the actual product
Serif headline with one clear button
Benefit pills list main reasons to choose
fixes: Nav links are faint over the photo
New location card crowds the hero
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero is a real photo of the storage corridor with numbered blue doors, and the headline says Storage that fits 24/7 London life. A visitor sees what they will rent and why it is easy. Find your space is the main button.

## What works
- The photo is the real product, so the page feels honest and distinct from generic storage sites.
- A row of short pills, such as No hidden costs and Late night access, lists benefits quickly.
- Location cards with a map, tube station walking times and a Book now button help a visitor choose.

## Where it is weak
- The menu links are pale and hard to read on top of the photo.
- A new location card in the hero competes with the main button, and on the phone it pushes content down.

## The lesson
Use a photo of your real product as the hero, and keep one main button clear of other offers.

title: Warm peach hero with a smiling resident
works: Warm peach band with serif headline
Large photo of a smiling resident and carer
Two clear paths: care or retirement living
fixes: Hero has no button for a first step
Purpose section is long plain text
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page feels warm before a visitor reads a word. A peach background, a red serif headline and a large photo of a resident with a carer set a kind tone. For a family choosing care, tone matters as much as facts.

## What works
- The photo shows real smiling people close up. It builds trust and feels personal.
- The serif headline in warm red is calm and clear. The spacing around it is generous.
- Two cards, long-term care and retirement living, each have a button. A visitor can pick the right path quickly.

## Where it is weak
- The hero has no button, so the first screen offers no next step.
- The Our Purpose section is long text with little for a family who wants to compare homes.

## The lesson
In a care page, use warm colour and a close human photo, then add a visible button to the first screen.

title: Warm home photo of a video doctor visit
works: Photo shows exactly how the visit works
One dark button: Book my appointment
Insurance logos remove the cost worry early
fixes: Photo fades into the page on laptop
Stat cards at the bottom feel small
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The hero photo shows a woman on a sofa at home talking with a doctor on a tablet. That one image explains the service. The serif headline says a virtual sleep clinic that helps you feel like yourself again, and Book my appointment is the only action.

## What works
- The picture and the headline both say care happens at home, so the offer is clear at once.
- A row of insurance names such as Anthem, Cigna and Medicare comes straight after the hero.
- A three step section, meet a specialist, take a home test, start treatment, makes the path plain.

## Where it is weak
- On a laptop, the photo edge blends softly into the page, so the hero looks a little undefined.
- The three number cards at the bottom use small icons and feel slight next to the headlines above.

## The lesson
Show the real service moment in the hero photo, and put the insurance logos right below it.

- A short line names who they help: technology, consumer, media and agency businesses.

title: Oxford college photo with serif headline
works: Oxford building photo sets the place at once
Serif type feels academic and calm
Four facts in a row under hero
fixes: Chat button covers text on phone
Course cards use small, pale text
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
A photo of an Oxford college building and a serif headline tell parents where the course is and what kind of school it is. Red buttons are the only strong colour, so the two ways to reach an advisor are clear.

## What works
- The hero photo shows the real location, which is what parents are paying for.
- A serif typeface and a restrained red give the page a traditional, trusted feel.
- Years running, alumni, nationalities and number of courses sit in one row under the hero.

## Where it is weak
- The green chat button sits over the facts row and covers text on the phone.
- Course cards show price and age in very small, light type.

## The lesson
Let one real photo of the place carry the hero, and put your proof numbers directly below it.

title: Aerial ranch photo under a serif headline
works: Full-width aerial photo sets the place
Two buttons: solid tour, outlined venues
Warm cream and brown palette feels consistent
fixes: White headline sits on a busy photo
Cookie icon overlaps the text on phone
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The first screen is a wide aerial photo of the ranch with white serif text on top: "Where California's natural beauty meets timeless elegance." Two buttons follow, a solid brown "Reserve a private tour" and an outlined "Explore the venues." Below, a photo of a couple at an arched door and a row of venue photos show the places a couple could book.

## What works
- The aerial photo shows the size and setting of the property, which is what a couple needs to see first.
- The solid button is the main action and the outlined one is the second choice. The same brown appears in the logo, the top bar and the buttons.
- Venue cards use large photos with the venue name over them, and the cream and sand backgrounds keep the page warm and quiet.

## Where it is weak
- The white headline runs across a busy photo of hills and trees, so some letters are harder to read.
- On the phone, a round cookie icon sits on top of the heading in the second section.

## The lesson
Lead with one large photo of the place itself, and give it one solid button and one quiet button.

title: Calm editorial layout with a full-bleed venue photo
works: Dusk hero photo sells the building
Serif intro line sets a refined tone
Capacity and features sit in clear columns
fixes: Phone hero shows only a name
Get in touch button is small and pale
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page treats the venue like a gallery. A large evening photo, a serif sentence about the setting and plenty of white space tell an event planner this is a premium room. Then the facts they need to shortlist it follow right away.

## What works
- The hero is a full-width photo of the glass building at dusk with only the venue name on it. It sells the look without clutter.
- The intro sentence in a large serif names the location and views. A single red "Take a virtual tour" button gives a clear first action.
- "The Details" lays out event styles, seated and cocktail capacities, key features and services in four columns. A planner can check fit without a phone call.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone the first screen shows only the name over a photo. There is no line about what the venue is or any button.
- The Get in touch buttons are thin outlines with small text. They are easy to miss next to the red tour button.

## The lesson
Put capacity, features and contact details in plain columns right under a strong photo, and make the phone hero carry a button.

title: Loud type and a rider photo
works: Heavy headline in cream on dark teal
Coral button repeats on every section
Three plain promises sit beside the button
fixes: Cookie box covers the hero photo
Product cards leave large empty space
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page uses one dark teal, one coral and one heavy typeface. A smiling cyclist in a helmet fills the right side of the hero, so a rider knows at once this insurer is for them.

## What works
- The headline "Protect your bike with Laka" is large and sets the brand name in coral italics. The product is clear in four words.
- Three ticked lines sit under the headline: zero excess, no depreciation, claims handled by bike experts. They answer the first questions a rider has.
- The coral "Get a quote" button appears in the header, the hero, the reasons block and both product cards. A visitor never has to look for it.

## Where it is weak
- The cookie box covers the lower right of the photo on laptop and takes most of the first phone screen.
- The Core and Complete cards have large blank areas, so the Core card looks unfinished next to Complete.

## The lesson
Pick one bold typeface and two colours, then repeat one button colour so the action is always in view.

title: Dark hero with real cars and one yellow button
works: Real photos of the actual fleet
Yellow button stands out on black
Press logos right below the hero
fixes: Phone headline overlaps the logo in the photo
Phone number button is hard to read on phone
lessons:
# Why this page wins leads
The page shows the real cars in the first screen and gives one clear action. A visitor sees what they can rent, who covered the company and a bright button, all before scrolling.

## What works
- The hero headline names the service, the city and the year in one line, and real cars fill the photo behind it.
- The yellow button is the only bright colour on the dark page, so the eye goes straight to it.
- A row of press logos sits right under the hero, which gives proof before the visitor reads more.

## Where it is weak
- On the phone, the headline runs over the logo in the photo and is hard to read.
- The phone number button on the phone hero is dim and partly cut off.
